root.note: ekklēsía, from ek ‘out’ and kaléō ‘to call’: the people called out to meet.

history: In Athens, the ekklēsía was the assembly of citizens, the people called out to vote. Early Christians writing in Greek used the word for their own gathering, and Church Latin took it as ecclesia. Spoken Latin then wore it down. The double c softened, the l turned into r, as it often does in Portuguese, and Old Portuguese wrote eigreja before the modern igreja. Spanish has iglesia, French église: the same word, each changed in its own way. English took a different word for the building, church, from Greek kyriakón, ‘of the Lord’. But it borrowed ecclesia for learned words like ecclesiastical. In every Portuguese town the main church is a igreja matriz.
historyEinfach: Igreja means ‘church’. The word comes from Greek ekklēsía, ‘a meeting of the people’. Latin took it: ecclesia. Over many centuries it changed into igreja. Spanish iglesia and French église come from the same word. English church comes from a different Greek word.

elsewhere.text: French also lost the first c and kept an l.
English named the building after the Lord, not after the people who meet in it.
